title: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Authentication Package
shortTitle: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Authentication Package
summary: Windows authentication packages are libraries loaded by the Local Security Authority process, lsass.exe, when the system starts, and they supply the logon processes and security protocols the operating system supports. The list of packages to load lives in a registry value named Authentication Packages under the Lsa key of the current control set. An adversary with administrator rights appends the path of their own library to that list, so the security process loads it at every boot, which yields persistence inside a highly privileged process and often a route to credential material handled by that process. The artefacts are registry writes to the Lsa value, image load telemetry where the security process loads a module from outside the system directory or without a valid signature, and boot-time module records that differ from the baseline. A default installation carries a small known set of Microsoft packages, so any additional entry is the discriminator; on Windows 8.1 and later, LSA protection can refuse unsigned modules and block the technique.

beginner.definition: This technique adds an attacker's library to a list that the Windows security process reads at startup. That process handles all sign in requests, and it loads a set of helper libraries to do its work. The list of helpers is stored in one registry value. An attacker adds their own library to the list. Then the security process loads the attacker's code inside itself at every boot. This sub-technique differs from its parent because the system start, and not a user sign in, sets off the code.
beginner.whyItMatters: The security process holds a very high level of trust, and the attacker's library runs inside it. That position can also expose sign in data that passes through the process. A single registry value keeps the code in place across restarts and updates. If you never check which libraries that process loads, this kind of persistence can stay hidden for a long time.
howItWorks: When Windows starts, a process called the Local Security Authority handles all sign in requests.
That process loads a set of helper libraries, called authentication packages, to do its work.
The list of libraries to load is stored in one registry value under the Lsa key.
An attacker adds the path of their own library to that list, which needs administrator rights.
At every boot the security process loads the library and runs the attacker's code inside itself.
Newer Windows versions can protect that process and refuse libraries without a valid signature.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital reception desk with a list of approved interpreters. Every morning the desk calls each person on the list to the front. If someone adds a stranger to the list, the desk calls that stranger every morning and gives them access to patient notes. Authentication packages are that list, and the security process is the desk that trusts it.
takeaways: Authentication packages are libraries that the Windows security process loads at boot.
One registry value adds an attacker's library to that trusted process.
LSA protection on newer Windows can block unsigned libraries in that process.

objectives: Explain what the Local Security Authority process does at system start.
Describe how the Authentication Packages registry value controls library loading.
Explain why execution inside that process is valuable to an attacker.
Identify the telemetry that shows modules loaded into that process.
Explain how a platform protection feature can block this technique.
Compare a default package list with a modified one.
